ff.plaques.1_raptor.title: Raptor
ff.plaques.1_raptor.body:
Small dromaeosaurid theropod with feathers and a large sickle-shaped claw on each hind foot. Native to Asia. Likely used claw for gripping prey rather than slashing. Carnivorous, fast, and agile.
Note: Skeleton scaled to match ficticious size from Jurassic Park movie franchise.
ff.plaques.1_bronto.title: Bronto
ff.plaques.1_bronto.body: Huge quadrupedal herbivore from western North America. Small head with peg-like teeth on a long, tapering neck. Massive, barrel-shaped body supported by four column-like limbs and a whip-like tail.
ff.plaques.1_t-rex.title: Scary Dino
ff.plaques.1_t-rex.body: Large apex theropod predator from western North America. Massive skull with bone-crushing bite force and serrated teeth. Bipedal with powerful hind limbs and reduced forelimbs. Carnivorous, likely both hunter and scavenger.
ff.plaques.1_dimetrodon.title: Dimetrodon
ff.plaques.1_dimetrodon.body: Large sail-backed synapsid, not a dinosaur. Apex predator of its ecosystems in what is now North America and Europe. Distinct elongated neural spines formed a dorsal sail, likely used for thermoregulation and display.
ff.plaques.1_trike.title: Pokey Dino
ff.plaques.1_trike.body: Large ceratopsian herbivore with three facial horns and a broad bony frill. Native to western North America. Likely used horns and frill for defense, display, and intraspecies combat. Fed on low-growing vegetation using a beak and shearing dental batteries.
ff.plaques.1_gold-shark.title: Gold Shark
ff.plaques.1_gold-shark.body: Rare variant of tiger shark found near river beds. Exhibits metallic gold coloration derived from ingesting yellow sweaters dropped by nearby players. Primary diet includes the Nautilus, with preference for “golden” individuals.
ff.plaques.1_deep-sea.title: Deep Sea
ff.plaques.1_deep-sea.body:
Nautilus:
Marine cephalopod with a coiled external shell divided into gas-filled chambers for buoyancy control.

Giant Tube Worms:
They thrive in extreme environments on the seafloor, particularly around hydrothermal vents in the Pacific Ocean.
ff.plaques.1_plesiosaur.title: Swim Dino
ff.plaques.1_plesiosaur.body: Marine reptiles with broad bodies, four large flippers, and often very long necks with small heads. Lived in oceans worldwide. Used flippers in a rowing motion for propulsion. Carnivorous, feeding on fish and cephalopods.
ff.plaques.1_footprints.title: Footprints
ff.plaques.1_footprints.body: Trace fossils preserving impressions of dinosaur feet in sediment. Formed when animals walked on soft ground that later lithified. Provide data on gait, speed, group movement, and behavior.
ff.plaques.ruins_basketball.title: Ruins Basketball
ff.plaques.ruins_basketball.body: The inhabitants of these ancient ruins are believed to love basketball. Fossilized statues recovered found them in positions consistent with the sport. It was theorized with their short height that for 45,000 years they roamed the overworld, but never scored a basket.
ff.plaques.ruins_wishing-well.title: Ruins Wishing Well
ff.plaques.ruins_wishing-well.body: An ancient and magical wishing well the copper inhabitants would use to get back home. Theorized to be a predecessor of the enderporter. The golems built wells across the overworld, when the sun started to set they would throw in a wishing coin, and the well would send them home.
ff.plaques.ruins_ruins.title: Outside
ff.plaques.ruins_ruins.body:
Ancient unrestored ruins, transported directly from the primordial grounds and the birthplace of the copper golem. 

Radiological dating and geological context suggests these ruins are approximately 100,000 years old.
ff.plaques.ruins_artifacts.title: Artifacts
ff.plaques.ruins_artifacts.body:
An ancient restored tower from the trail ruins. 

Likely a religious temple for the inhabitants, the tower displayed mysterious patterns that is postulated to hold their deepest of secrets.
ff.plaques.ruins_ancient-cities.title: Ancient Cities
ff.plaques.ruins_ancient-cities.body: The copper golem exclusively built their ruins on top of ancient cities, in deep dark biomes. Rumour had it the sculk provided rich nutrients to the soil for agriculture, while other archaeologists beleived it was for protection of their deepest treasures.
ff.plaques.ruins_fishing.title: Fishing
ff.plaques.ruins_fishing.body:
The copper golems primary food source was spinach & ricotta stuffed salmon fillet, served over warm rice with a side of garlic bread. 

Of course this is only an assumption... based on the fact that we found water near their homes.
ff.plaques.ruins_crops.title: Crops
ff.plaques.ruins_crops.body:
While the other societies of golems had their elaborate meals, the jungle golems subsisted on a simpler diet of potatoes and various fruits from the rainforest.

Some evidence of riverine fish consumption is also noted.
ff.plaques.ruins_jungle-temple.title: Jungle Temple
ff.plaques.ruins_jungle-temple.body:
These reclusive rainforest temples were created as tombs by a different culture of copper golems, which due to the humidity of their environment oxidized faster. 

Researchers theorize they held death as a more important role in society as a result.
ff.plaques.ruins_pots.title: Pots
ff.plaques.ruins_pots.body:
Ancient Pots with symbols carved by the copper golems. 

It is believed they were stored underground and the moistness of the sculk kept the pots from cracking, while the warden guarded the pots and their secrets.
ff.plaques.ruins_ancient-portal.title: Scary Portal
ff.plaques.ruins_ancient-portal.body:
Once suspected to be part of an ancient portal, this mysterious block has long puzzled explorers. Forgotten by time, its original purpose and the people who created it remain unknown.

Whether it was truly a portal or something else entirely is still a mystery.
ff.plaques.2_the-human.title: The Human
ff.plaques.2_the-human.body:
The Human


     (Homo Sapiens)





        Written by
   Dr. SirSpacewalker




We build. We dig. We craft. 


No claws, no wings, no natural armor; yet we reshape entire worlds with nothing but our hands and a few sticks.




The human is a strange creature.


Soft-bodied and slow, it should not survive.


And yet, it is the most dominant species on the planet.


Other beings wander. The jellyfish drifts without purpose; the amsel collects in silence. The dog shuffles forward, forgetting what it once was. 

But the human builds toward something, always something just beyond the horizon.



They say life is simple. But watch one long enough and you'll see it's not. Watch them create new life. 

Watch them go where no other human has gone yet. Watch them fight over and over again for what they think is right.




There is no potion that gives them wings, so they build towers instead. 


Every limitation is just a problem waiting for a crafting table; the sky is definitely not one of them.



In the end, they reach the impossible - they always reach the impossible. 


Not because they were the strongest species in the world, but because they refused to stop building until they were...

The history of the human will continue.
ff.plaques.2_ankylo.title: Ankylo
ff.plaques.2_ankylo.body: Heavily armored herbivore with osteoderm plates and a large bony tail club. Native to western North America. Tail likely used for high-force defensive strikes against predators. Low browsing diet using a beak and leaf-shaped teeth.
ff.plaques.2_sniffer.title: Minecraft Dino
ff.plaques.2_sniffer.body: The Sniffer is an ancient, gentle creature from Minecraft. Once thought to be extinct, it was rediscovered by archaeologists. The Sniffer has an extraordinary sense of smell and enjoys finding ancient seeds buried beneath the ground.
ff.plaques.2_burrowers.title: Big Rats
ff.plaques.2_burrowers.body:
Many species of insects adapted to niches situated within and involving trees.

These niches would be later shared to some capacity with the first mammals, resembling the habitat of modern -day squirrels.
ff.plaques.2_fossils.title: Fossils
ff.plaques.2_fossils.body: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of plants and animals that lived long ago. They can form from bones, shells, footprints, and even leaves. Fossils help scientists learn about ancient life and understand how Earth has changed over millions of years.
ff.plaques.3_hadean.title: Hadean
ff.plaques.3_hadean.body:
The Hadean was defined by intense bombardment of the ancient, forming Earth.

One of these ancient collisions was with a protoplanet named Theia, which collided wih Earth to form the Moon.

The surface was largely molten, and

slowly cooled into the Archean. Heavier elements like iron and nickel sank to the core, while lighter silicas rose to form the crust.

Very small zircon crystals from this eon have been preserved, but no known rocks survived from this time of history.
ff.plaques.3_archean.title: Archean
ff.plaques.3_archean.body:
The Archean was dominated by empty, vast oceans spanning most of the globe. High volcanism and plate tectonics gradually created the first ancient landmasses.

Life started in this Eon, with unicellular organisms deep in the seas.

The Archean atmosphere was vastly different to that of the present; methane rich, it would be more similar to Titan's atmosphere, a light hazy orange.

Asteroid impacts gradually slowed over the early Archean, to lower levels.
ff.plaques.3_proterozoic.title: Proterozoic
ff.plaques.3_proterozoic.body:
The Proterozoic saw the rise of cyanobacteria, which lowered CO2 levels and released O2 - sparking the Great Oxygenation. 

The skies slowly turned blue, and this change in chemistry of the air also affected the water. Iron precipitated out

of the water to settle on the seafloors, later becoming banded iron formations that form the majority of mineable iron today.

The Proterozoic saw 2 ice ages, the Huronian and Cryogenian. The Huronian occured because of the Great Oxygenation removing CO2 from the air,

lasting over 300 million years.

The Cryogenian, also known as Snowball Earth, saw the Earth (nearly) covered by ice towards the end of the Proterozoic. 

The Ediacaran Period at the end of this Eon saw the first large multicellular 

organisms, a trend that would spark the Cambrian Explosion of aquatic life.
ff.plaques.3_cambrian.title: Cambrian
ff.plaques.3_cambrian.body:
The Cambrian commences the Phanerozoic Eon - also known as the Eon of Life. 

The Cambrian Explosion starts by most metrics the fossil record, when a sudden increase in ancient marine fossils permeated the rock record.

One of the most known specimens from this time was the trilobite. 

Named for having 3 distinct sections, the trilobite is a common arthopod class that persisted for hundreds of millions of years until the Permian-Triassic Extinction.
ff.plaques.3_ordovician.title: Ordovician
ff.plaques.3_ordovician.body:
The Ordovician saw a continuation of the evolution of large, multicellular life from the Cambrian.

One of the most famous genuses of this period, Endoceras, was a group of nautiloids that grew to enormous sized, their shells over 3 metres long.

The Ordovician was also characterized by unusual bombardment within 30° of latitude to the equator; possibly signifying that Earth had a ring system for the duration of the bombardment period.

This may have sparked a mass extinction & ice age.
ff.plaques.3_silurian.title: Silurian
ff.plaques.3_silurian.body:
The Silurian saw warming from the Hirnantian Glaciation. 

Jawed fish and sharks began to evolve at this time, and some sea creatures started to be more recognizable to us today.

The Late Silurian saw the Terrestrial Revolution, where

plants - and later animals - found niches on land and developed terrestrial ecosystems. While some species had migrated to land in the Ordovician, the Late Silurian is when most did so.

Fungi were some of the first to make that transition.
ff.plaques.3_devonian.title: Devonian
ff.plaques.3_devonian.body:
The Early Devonian saw the rise of prototaxites and other fungi* rise as the dominant terrestrial life. 

As plants began to adapt, they encroached on the niches of the fungi, slowly greening the Earth's land surface to one more

recognizable today.

The Late Devonian saw a series of extinctions, which together comprise one of the 5 "Big" Extinctions of Earth. It mainly affected the oceans, and the cause is unknown.

*Prototaxites are debated in their placement within the tree of life. Some refer to it as a fungus, others consider it its own unique, extinct kingdom like plants, animals, and fungi.
ff.plaques.3_carboniferous.title: Carboniferous
ff.plaques.3_carboniferous.body:
The Carboniferous, meaning "Coal-Bearing" in Latin, is defined by the rich coal seams that permeate the rocks today from this period. 

Oxygen-depleted swamps with high plant growth led to biomass accumulating in these swamps, which would

form peat. This peat was then lithified into coal over subsequent periods.

The whole of the Carboniferous took place during an ice age, where the tropics and temperate areas are what we often picture from this period.

Pangea started forming during this period.

Oxygen levels rose to 35%, meaning animal life could grow to gargantuan sizes, particularly insects.

Fires were much more dangerous because of the extra oxygen.
ff.plaques.3_permian.title: Permian
ff.plaques.3_permian.body:
The Early Permian was a continuation of the Carboniferous, with the gradual decline of the long ice age that defined the last 2 periods.

Conifers, having evolved in the Late Carboniferous, proliferated and spread widely in the Permian.

The Permian was marked by several extinctions, of which the two largest took place near the end of the period.

The Capitanian Extinction (~260 Mya) was likely caused by the Emeishan Traps, a large volcanic region in Sichuan, China.

Not long after, the Permian-Triassic Extinction, also known as the Great Dying, took place at 251.9 Mya.

A similar cause, this time it was the Siberian Traps that let loose vast fields of lava, polluting the atmosphere and acidifying the oceans.

It's theorized the ozone layer was severely damaged, due to recorded biological damage in fossils. It was the worst extinction in history, and took millions of years to recover from.

The Trilobite finally went extinct at this time.
ff.plaques.3_triassic.title: Triassic
ff.plaques.3_triassic.body:
The Triassic was the hottest period of Earth in the Phanerozoic. 

After the End-Permian Extinction, global temperatures were elevated due to the excess greenhouse gasses and Pangea's land configuration blocking moisture from the land's interior.

While present in some of the Permian, megamonsoons formed in the Panthalassic Ocean around Pangea and impacted the tropical areas with monumental intensity.

Triassic climate was extreme. The Carnian Pluvial Episode was a 2 million year event where rainfall and

humidity affected almost the entire world; this sudden climactic shift is possibly related to the rise of the dinosaurs.

The climate dried again after the Carnian. The rifting of Pangea would lead to new volcanism in the heart of the super-

-continent, slowly forming the Atlantic. 

The volcanism would trigger the Triassic-Jurassic Extinction, with similar but less-extreme impacts to the Permian-Triassic Extinction at the start of the period.
ff.plaques.3_jurassic.title: Jurassic
ff.plaques.3_jurassic.body:
The Jurassic quickly rebounded from the mass extinction at its start, and as Pangea slowly started to break apart the temperatures of the planet cooled - though still far warmer than today.

The Jurassic only had one large extinction after this, when

the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event occured 183 Mya, as oxygen levels in the oceans plummeted.

While there were dinosaurs in the Triassic, they grew more plentiful and diverse in the Jurassic.

The Pangean megamonsoon began to wane during the Jurassic as the supercontinent broke into Laurasia and Gondwana.

The breakup of the continents would lead to greater biodiversity going into the Cretaceous, and modern day.
ff.plaques.3_cretaceous.title: Cretaceous
ff.plaques.3_cretaceous.body:
The Cretaceous was a time of massive change. Pangea finally broke apart completely, the Atlantic Ocean was opening while the Tethys was closing, and continents slowly began to take their modern forms.

Many continents were partially submerged,

case in point being North America. The central region, what would become the Prairies / Great Plains, flooded to form a biodiverse inland sea which resulted in many of the inland fossils seen in places like Alberta, Canada.

Flowering plants diversified and took

over many of the gymnosperms' niches (ferns, conifers, etc).

The most famous dinosaurs existed in the Cretaceous, including the Velociraptor and T-Rex.

Forests were present at the poles, and snow was restricted to 

mountain peaks.

The Cretaceous may be most famous for what ended it. The K-Pg extinction, the 5th and most recent mass extinction, resultant from the Chicxulub Asteroid and possibly assisted by the volcanic Deccan Traps in India.
ff.plaques.3_paleogene.title: Paleogene
ff.plaques.3_paleogene.body:
The Paleogene was a time of climate transition. The K-Pg mass extinction 66 Mya had brief but devastating effects, cooling global temperatures and shrouding the skies.

Not long after, however, came the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, or 

PETM. The PETM warmed the world drastically, with an unknown cause. Precipitation increased, but some dry areas remained.

The PETM is considered a way to study recent and replicatable climate change in the past, and is seen as a

worst case scenario for Anthropogenic climate change.

Millions of years after, the planet began to cool as Antarctica separated and moved to the south pole, allowing ocean currents to isolate it and build up cold temperatures.

This sparked the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, ongoing today.

Many modern plants and animals can trace their ancestors to diversifying in the Paleogene.

The Paleogene and Neogene were once considered the Tertiary Period.
ff.plaques.3_neogene.title: Neogene
ff.plaques.3_neogene.body:
The Neogene is the penultimate period of the Phanerozoic eon, and during it the continents began to take their current shape today.

India was in the midst of colliding with Asia, Panama connected the Americas, Japan rifted from Asia, etc.

The Paleogene was marked by glacial and interglacial periods. One of those interglacials, the Pliocene Thermal Maximum (≈3.0 Mya) is viewed as a possibly middling-scenario for Anthropogenic climate change, in contrast to the more severe warming of the Eocene.

The Messinian Salinity Crisis 5.5 Mya saw most of the Mediterranean dry up, as tectonics forced Spain and Morocco together.

Temperatures as high as 80°C may have occured in the basin, until erosion released the Atlantic back

into the former sea in what was known as the Zanclean flood, carving the Strait of Gibraltar in only a matter of years.
ff.plaques.3_quaternary.title: Quaternary
ff.plaques.3_quaternary.body:
The Quaternary is the current geologic period, divided into the Pleistocene and Holocene.

The Pleistocene is what most people picture hearing the phrase "Ice Age," or at least the last glacial maximum of it.

Ice sheets covered

much of North America and Europe, which periodically advanced and reteated in accordance with changes in how Earth orbits the Sun, called Milankovitch Cycles. 

These ice sheets formed basins which filled with water, forming the Great Lakes and other 

water bodies like the Baltic Sea. Sea levels rose and fall depending on how much water was stored as ice sheets.

Early human species diversified in Africa, and learned how to use fire. They later spread across the world during the Last Glacial Maximum.

While different societies developed agriculture at different times, the Neolithic Revolution is considered to have happened around 10 years ago.

In those 10K years, humans (now only Homo Sapiens) began to dominate the planet. While some argue that

our impact has been enough to classify recent history as a new geologic period (the Anthropocene) this proposal was rejected.

Nevertheless we have impacted Earth on the scale of the mass extinctions, and as I hope you can appreciate from my

timeline, in the blink of an eye geologically.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This timeline has been a passion project for me and my academic studies, so I hope you enjoyed it!
